name: Pale Purple
lede: Pale purple is a descriptive name: a light, soft purple that dictionaries use to define lilac, thistle and other named shades.

sections.title: A description more than a name
sections.body: The books use the phrase mostly to describe other colors. Paterson defines [[lilac]] as the pale purple of lilac blossom, and [[thistle]] as a very pale purple, one of the 140 X11 colors with hex code #D8BFD8 [1][2]. The same dictionary uses it for *vistal*, an old word for a pale purple [3]. The words are the same each time; the shade is not.

sections.title: Pale purple in nature
sections.body: Baty's *Nature's Palette* [4] matches Werner's color names to flowers, butterflies and minerals. The pale purple primrose and the light spots on a peacock butterfly's wings sit under Werner's lavender purple, beside the mineral lepidolite [4]. Pigment sources use the phrase for a mineral too: the rare iron phosphate purpurite is described as ranging from pale purple to dark red [5]. See also [[lavender]] and [[wisteria]].

sections.title: Mixing it
sections.body: St Clair uses pale purple as her example of why painters struggle with mixing: with impure pigments, a pale purple needs at least a red, a blue and a white, and the result can easily turn dull [6]. A pale purple is, in practice, a purple pushed toward white while keeping the red-blue balance. Compare [[purple]] and [[lavender-blue]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our name graph records this swatch in the ISCC-NBS descriptive scheme of 1955 and in the 2010 xkcd survey [7].

No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering at least 1 per cent of its canvas, within a CIEDE2000 distance of 4, as photographed [8]. That describes this archive, not painting as a whole [8].
